Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Idealized Families: Happy families, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mai sits rigidly in her chair, her hands clasped so tightly in her lap that her knuckles are white. At thirty-eight, she is a successful stockbroker, a master of calculated risks and market analysis, yet for the past two years, her own life has felt like an exercise in pure, unmanageable chaos. It all began with her ex-boyfriend, a period she now struggles to speak about. The relationship had ended, but he hadn't accepted it. For six months, he stalked her, a campaign of psychological terror fueled by alcohol. He would leave rambling, maudlin voicemails one hour and appear outside her apartment the next, his breath thick with the smell of whiskey. He would bang on her door at all hours, the sudden, explosive sound making her heart seize in her chest. In his distorted view, their breakup was a temporary hurdle; he would send her saccharine photos of happy families torn from magazines, with notes scrawled on the back: "This could be us. We are meant for this." The memory of it all, even now, feels profoundly strange, so extreme and cinematic that Mai sometimes finds it hard to believe it actually happened to her. It feels like a story about someone else.

That feeling of unreality vanishes, however, the moment a memory is triggered. The past doesn't just return; it consumes the present. Last week, on the trading floor, the closing bell rang just as a colleague behind her shouted a trade. The combination of loud, sudden noises sent a shockwave through her. In an instant, she was no longer in her office tower in downtown Manhattan; she was back in her old apartment, cowering in the dark, listening to the splintering sound of his fist against her front door. The terror was not a memory of fear, but the raw, visceral experience of it, flooding her body as if it were happening all over again. She had to grip the edge of her desk to keep from screaming, her screen of flashing numbers blurring into a meaningless wash of red and green.

Her life has since become a careful map of avoidance. The high-pressure, boisterous culture of her firm, once a source of adrenaline, is now a minefield. She has started wearing noise-canceling headphones for most of the day, a move that has isolated her from the team and earned a concerned comment from her manager. The social fabric of her career was woven in after-work drinks, but Mai can no longer tolerate being in a bar. The scent of stale beer or the sharp smell of liquor on someone's breath is enough to make her stomach clench with nausea and her mind fill with the image of his face, flushed and angry. She makes excuses, citing deadlines or fatigue, but feels her professional relationships fraying with each declined invitation. Even her home, a sanctuary with her new partner, is not entirely safe. A walk in the park on a sunny Sunday can be ruined by the sight of a family laughing on a picnic blanket. For Mai, the image is no longer one of joy, but a grotesque parody tainted by her stalker's delusional letters, a trigger that fills her with a confusing mix of dread and disgust.

These reactions have built a wall around her, one her current partner, David, struggles to understand. He sees her recoil when he opens a beer after a long day, sees the vacant look in her eyes when a car backfires on the street below their window. She has tried to explain, but the story feels too unreal in the telling, the words inadequate to convey the persistent, living nature of the threat inside her mind. The breaking point came after a recent performance review, where her boss described her as "distracted" and "chronically on edge." The fear of losing the career she had built with such fierce determination was finally greater than the fear of confronting the past. Mai came to therapy because she is terrified that the ghost of one man will succeed in destroying not just her peace of mind, but her future, her relationship, and the very identity she has fought so hard to protect.
